errors.english: because a perishing agent does not remain precisely because it remains as itself
errors.why: The reason is that when the destroyer is not present the thing remains of itself; the English makes the destroyer the subject of a self-contradictory clause.

errors.english: In the ultimate sense, that which dwells in the object does not even meet with the object.
errors.why: Ultimately [the mind] neither abides in the object nor meets the object; the abiding is negated too, not made the subject.
Here ཉེ་བར་ལེན་པ is upādāna as material cause (as just used of fuel and lamp): this transformation is the faultless definition of a material cause, not of 'appropriation'.

note: Follows the commentary in outline, but several argument steps in the perishing/support refutation are garbled.

errors.english: Regarding the connection with the essential nature of the (dharmin) the subject of the argument
errors.why: In this list of thesis faults the item is contradiction with the subject's own nature (dharmisvarūpaviparīta, the e-text's འབྲེལ standing for འགལ), as the space example shows; 'connection' misnames the fallacy.

note: A sound rendering of the discussion of svayam in the thesis definition; one fallacy name misread.
Faithful word-by-word gloss commentary on the tigress episode; only cosmetic transliteration glitches.

errors.english: For the act of requesting and dual actions
errors.why: These are the standard Vinaya act types: an act with a motion only, an act of motion and one proclamation (jñaptidvitīya), an act of motion and three proclamations (jñapticaturtha); 'requesting and dual/fourfold actions' misrenders them.

errors.english: abiding completely refers to practicing pure conduct
errors.why: ཡོངས་སུ་གནས་པ here is the monk under probation (pārivāsika), as the next side's quotation (expelling a monk) shows; 'abiding completely' loses the Vinaya status.

note: Usable outline of the karmavācanā discussion, but Vinaya technical vocabulary is handled loosely and the argument is hard to follow.

errors.english: the head of the milkman thrown by the hand of peace
errors.why: ཞོ་རྫིའུ is a curd pot thrown by Śivā's hand that falls on the head, not a milkman.

fix.find: the head of the milkman thrown by the hand of peace
fix.replace: the head: the curd pot thrown by the hand of Śivā

errors.english: the mother of Gopala will know it through peace itself
errors.why: ཞི་བ is the name of Gopāla's mother (Śivā), the agent, not the abstract 'peace'.

errors.english: From the direction of the Chilikun Lake
errors.why: སྤྱི་བླུགས is 'water-pot' (kamaṇḍalu/kuṇḍikā); 'Chilikun' is an invented form, not a name in the text.

note: The lexical glosses are mostly followed, but the narrative names and objects in the story are mistranslated.

errors.english: Through that, i.e., through its nature, how could one logically deduce, "If it changes from a specific nature, why would this also not change?" It is not logical to deduce that entities are possessed of a person's desire.
errors.why: The Tibetan says the consequence IS properly pressed against things governed by nature, but NOT against things dependent on human intention; the English turns the first into a denial and misparses the second.

fix.find: Through that, i.e., through its nature, how could one logically deduce, "If it changes from a specific nature, why would this also not change?" It is not logical to deduce that entities are possessed of a person's desire.
fix.replace: Against those it is proper to press the consequence through that, i.e., through their nature: "Since it occurs from a specific nature, why would it not occur in this case too?" But it is not proper to press such a consequence against things that depend on a person's intention.

errors.english: Having made such an assertion, it is because of intending it in that way.
errors.why: It is because the maker of the convention (the mantra-maker, cf. previous side) so intended; the agent is lost.

note: The mantra-efficacy argument is mostly tracked, but the key contrast between natural and intention-dependent things is inverted.
Faithful and careful rendering of the observation/non-observation and substance/quality presentation.

errors.english: Their reversal is the non-existence of non-perception.
errors.why: The absence of those (cognition and object) is non-perception, i.e. absence; the English inverts it into the absence of non-perception.

errors.english: Since it is possible for a cause to exist without the result, this also thoroughly expresses the answer to the claim that
errors.why: 'A cause can exist without its result' is part of the opponent's objection being answered, not the author's premise.

note: Sound overall on the non-perception argument; two clauses misassigned.

errors.english: These phenomena are neither with affliction nor without affliction.
errors.why: The sūtra says these phenomena are without affliction, not afflicted; it does not deny that they are without affliction.

fix.find: These phenomena are neither with affliction nor without affliction.
fix.replace: These phenomena are without affliction; they are not afflicted.

note: Good rendering of the Madhyamaka argument and the Akṣayamati quotation, with one inverted sentence.

errors.english: That itself is not a species.
errors.why: The root verse says this is not in accord with reality (tattva); རིགས here is 'fitting/reasonable', not 'species', as the commentary's དེ་ཉིད་རིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ shows.

fix.find: That itself is not a species.
fix.replace: It is not in accord with reality.

errors.english: error without a seed will not occur even in those who appear perversely
errors.why: A seedless error, i.e. an erroneous appearance, would not arise; 'perverse appearance' qualifies the error, not some persons.
སྤྱོད here is inquiry/discourse (cintā) about external objects: the Buddhas, adopting the world's view, engage in discussion of externals, not 'external behavior'.

note: Follows the elephant's-gaze passage, but the root verse is misread and several clauses are opaque.
